activity.title: Hey guys, I'm very excited to give you a little look into what I’ve been working on with Sathwik Nemani and Keerthi Kaashyap ! We noticed that B2B support channels often get cluttered and information transfer is highly manual/laborious, leading to lost information, breached SLAs, and longer resolution times. Whiteboard is a platform that intelligently extracts and synthesizes data from a wide variety of sources such as conversations, knowledge bases, code, etc. into a unified searchable framework to improve the efficiency of your customer support pipeline. Here's a peek into our conversation-to-ticketing workflow for Slack, so your team never has to spend hours manually filtering through 10s or 100s of Slack channels for customers issues. Interested in trying Whiteboard? Join our waitlist: https://tally.so/r/w5qEbN Sign up for a demo: https://lnkd.in/dby4pTUR We’d love to get your feedback and iterate alongside you and your team! Hey everyone! I am so happy and grateful to launch Weave’s beta today with Sashank and Sathwik ! In one line, Weave is an app that autodetects your screenshots and uses AI to find relevant links from screenshots and makes them actionable. Think about all screenshots you take - images of reels or TikToks of good restaurants in your area, Twitter bookmarks, products you buy or a long list of links. All these images just gather virtual dust in your Photos library! The biggest problem is that these screenshots are not actionable upon. If I had to use any of the images I stated above, I’d actually have to open a browser, type my query again and surf to get to my link. Weave seamlessly detects your screenshots from your Photos folder, filters away sensitive and private images, and contextually understands the rest to find relevant links to your images. For example, a marketplace site for a product you want to buy, the Maps/Reservation/Web link to a reel of the best mexican restaurants in NYC and so on. Please sign up for our beta here: https://www.weave.team ...more ...more

This past spring, I presented a poster at UC Riverside's Undergraduate Research Symposium on multimodal RAG over 5G specifications. It was the end of about a year of work: finding the problem, learning the fundamentals, building the thing, then rebuilding the parts I got wrong. 5G specs run thousands of pages, dense with diagrams and tables. I built a retrieval pipeline over them and tested what actually works on documentation that dense. The main comparison was between two ways of handling figures. One embeds images and text together in a single shared space. The other has a vision model describe every figure in plain text, then embeds only that. The whole thing runs on open weights in the 3 to 4 billion parameter range, locally with Ristretto-3B doing the figure descriptions, nomic-embed-text and CLIP as the two embedding paths, and Qwen and Gemma as base models, served through Ollama and Weaviate in Docker. I used small models deliberately so the results reflect the retrieval pipeline, not the raw strength of a frontier model. Scored against the ORAN-Bench-13K benchmark, the text-grounded approach won clearly. For specs this text-heavy, cross-modal comparison mostly introduces noise. Keyword search also carried more weight than I expected, and the two embedding types responded to query blending in opposite directions, which points to dynamic tuning per query. I'm continuing this work in the lab, in two directions. First, better evaluation: multiple-choice accuracy only tells you a system picked the right answer, not whether it actually understood the spec, so I'm looking at stronger evaluation strategies. Second, agentic capabilities: moving past answering questions about the spec toward actually applying it, using what the pipeline retrieves to reason about real codebases and real deployment scenarios. A poster makes a year look a lot more linear than it was. Funded and guided by the UCR Chancellor's Research Fellowship , with thanks to my PI, Dr. Zhaowei Tan .

SF is ambitious, but not aspirational. I will say it: Most founders I meet do not truly care about bringing value. You can tell because the gravitational pull of conversation goes towards capturing wealth, not creating it. You know the talk. Who raised the latest round, the trends VC’s will overvalue your company on, the hottest companies. There is a certain glee, a gold rush frenzy. They are still smart, and still work day and night (or so they claim). Some of them will succeed, massively. But every founder I talk to with a truly solid company - the kind of company that will probably still be around in 5 years - lies on the value side of the equation. In a world where people focus entirely on growing fast (and of course, I care about this too), what I’m really interested in is: who will still be around in 5, 10, 50 years? - The photo is with some founders Roop Pal Puneet Sukhija I know will be around :)
